title: Git Branching, Pull Requests, Code Review, and CI
description: Work safely in feature branches, keep pull requests reviewable, resolve conflicts deliberately, and use continuous integration as a repeatable quality gate.
learningOutcomes: Explain why feature branches separate work before integration.
Create and publish a focused branch and keep it synchronized with the base branch.
Prepare a reviewable pull request with context, testing evidence, and a small logical diff.
Review code for correctness, readability, accessibility, testing, and regressions.
Resolve merge conflicts deliberately and understand merge versus rebase at a high level.
Explain how CI runs automated checks and why a green check is not a substitute for review.
Compare common branch strategies and apply Semantic Versioning to compatible and breaking changes.
Resolve an active merge or rebase conflict by staging the intended result and continuing or aborting the correct operation.

blocks.text: Branches let work evolve before integration

A branch is a movable reference to a commit, which makes it possible to develop an isolated change without immediately altering the shared base branch. A feature branch should represent a coherent unit of work: a fix, feature, migration, or content update. Branches are lightweight, but unintegrated branches can drift, so keep the scope understandable and integrate when the change is ready.

blocks.code:
git switch main
git pull --ff-only origin main
git switch -c feat/search-empty-state
# make and test the change
git status
git add src/features/search
 git commit -m "fix(search): handle empty results"
git push -u origin feat/search-empty-state

steps.title: Start from an up-to-date base
steps.explanation: Switch to the intended base and update it. --ff-only prevents an accidental merge commit when the local branch diverges; inspect the situation if it fails.

steps.title: Create an isolated branch
steps.explanation: The branch name communicates both the type and purpose of the work. Keep names concise and scoped.

steps.title: Inspect and record a focused change
steps.explanation: Check the working tree, stage intended paths, and create a message describing one logical change. Before committing, inspect the staged diff if more than one task is present.

steps.title: Publish the branch for collaboration
steps.explanation: The first push publishes the commits to origin and sets upstream tracking for future updates.

blocks.text: A pull request is a review conversation

A useful pull request explains why the change is needed, what changed, how it was tested, and what reviewers should pay attention to. Keep the diff narrow enough to understand. Separate unrelated formatting, dependency updates, and behavior changes where practical. Screenshots or short recordings help when the change affects UI. If a PR is still experimental, mark it draft so others do not mistake it for ready-to-merge work.

blocks.caption: A concise PR template
blocks.code:
## Why
What user or maintenance problem does this solve?

## What changed
- Main behavior or design change

## Validation
- [ ] Lint / typecheck / tests / build
- [ ] Manual checks and screenshots if relevant

## Risks or follow-up
Anything reviewers should know.

blocks.text: Review for behavior, not personal style

A review should look for incorrect behavior, edge cases, unsafe data handling, inaccessible interactions, missing tests, confusing abstractions, and maintainability risks. Distinguish must-fix defects from optional suggestions and explain the impact. Use the project's formatter and lint rules to resolve style debates mechanically. The author remains responsible for understanding the final code; a reviewer should not approve code they do not understand just to move the queue along.
Merge and rebase: same goal, different history shape

Merge combines histories and may create a merge commit when branches have diverged. Rebase replays commits on top of a new base, producing a more linear history but rewriting commit IDs. Do not rebase shared commits that teammates may already depend on unless the team explicitly uses that workflow. Choose the project convention and never force-push a shared branch casually; if a force push is required after rebasing your own branch, prefer the safer lease check.
Resolve merge conflicts by understanding both changes

A conflict means Git cannot decide how to combine overlapping edits automatically. Open the conflicted files, understand the intention of both sides, edit the result, remove conflict markers, then run status and inspect the diff. Run relevant tests before continuing. Do not resolve a conflict by blindly choosing ours or theirs for an entire file if doing so would discard legitimate work.
CI repeats the project checks for every change

Continuous integration runs automated checks in a clean, repeatable environment, commonly on every pull request and push. A frontend pipeline may install dependencies from the lockfile, run linting, type checking, tests, and a production build. A green status means those configured checks passed at the tested commit; it does not prove all requirements are correct, replace manual QA, or validate a different commit pushed afterward. Investigate the actual failing job/log instead of rerunning blindly.

blocks.caption: Repository-aligned workflow: Node 22, lockfile-matched npm, least-privilege permissions, and the same CI checks
blocks.code:
name: Continuous Integration

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - name: Use the npm version used to generate the lockfile
        run: npm install --global npm@11.21.1
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Report npm audit advisories (informational)
        if: success()
        continue-on-error: true
        run: |
          npm audit --json > "$RUNNER_TEMP/npm-audit.json" || true
          node scripts/summarize-npm-audit.mjs "$RUNNER_TEMP/npm-audit.json"
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build

blocks.title: CI secrets and protected branches need care
blocks.text: Do not print secret values in workflow logs or expose repository credentials to untrusted pull-request code. Protect important branches with review and required checks. A workflow file itself is code and should be reviewed for permissions, untrusted inputs, and external action versions.

blocks.prompt: What makes a pull request easier and safer to review?

options.text: A focused diff with context and evidence that relevant checks passed
options.feedback: A narrow, well-explained change gives reviewers a clear scope and a way to verify it.

options.text: Combining several unrelated tasks into one huge diff
options.feedback: Unrelated changes make it harder to understand scope and catch regressions.

options.text: Removing tests so the PR has fewer lines
options.feedback: Tests provide evidence about behavior and reduce the risk of regressions.

options.text: Merging without checking CI because local development worked
options.feedback: The shared CI environment checks the submitted commit under the configured pipeline.

blocks.explanation: A reviewable PR is scoped, explained, and accompanied by evidence of validation.

blocks.prompt: Rebasing rewrites commit IDs because commits are recreated on a different base.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Rebase replays commits, and the rewritten commits have new identities.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Rebase creates new commit objects on top of the target base rather than preserving each original commit identity.

blocks.explanation: Because rebase changes history, coordinate with collaborators and avoid rewriting commits other people already use.

blocks.prompt: What should be part of a responsible pull-request workflow? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect the diff and run relevant checks
options.feedback: The diff and checks provide evidence that the proposed change is intentional and validated.

options.text: Resolve conflicts by understanding both sides
options.feedback: A conflict represents competing edits; understand the intended combined result before proceeding.

options.text: Expose secrets to pull-request code so tests can access everything
options.feedback: Untrusted code must not receive secrets unnecessarily.

options.text: Treat CI success as proof that no manual review is needed
options.feedback: CI covers configured checks but does not replace code review or all manual QA.

blocks.explanation: Safe collaboration combines focused changes, review, tests, explicit conflict resolution, and protected credentials.

blocks.title: Prepare and review a feature pull request
blocks.context: Use a personal or practice repository. The lesson editor stores your notes but does not execute Git commands.
instructions: Update your base branch and create a named feature branch.
Make a small change with one logical purpose and inspect the diff.
Run the project's lint, typecheck, tests, and production build commands that are configured.
Commit with a focused message and push the branch.
Open a PR with why, what changed, validation evidence, and any known risks.
Review the PR as a teammate: identify one risk, one improvement, and one positive observation.
If the branch becomes stale, integrate the base according to the project's merge/rebase convention and resolve conflicts carefully.
Confirm required CI checks apply to the latest commit before marking the change ready to merge.
requirements: The branch and commit have a single, explainable purpose.
The PR scope and testing evidence are documented.
The diff contains no accidental secrets, generated dependencies, or unrelated edits.
Relevant configured checks are run and their result is recorded.
Review feedback is specific, actionable, and respectful.
The learner can explain how the project handles conflicts and branch updates.
blocks.starterCode:
# Example checklist (use your repository's actual branch names)
git status
git switch main
git pull --ff-only origin main
git switch -c feat/meaningful-change

# make one focused change, then inspect it
git diff
git status

# stage only intended files and inspect the staged snapshot
git add src/
git diff --cached
git commit -m "feat: describe one meaningful change"
git push -u origin feat/meaningful-change

# Open a PR, document validation, review CI, and request review.
hints: Keep the PR smaller than a whole week's worth of unrelated work.
Read the CI failure's exact step and log before changing code.
When a conflict appears, read both sides and run tests after creating the resolved file.
successCriteria: The branch starts from the intended base and represents one logical change.
The PR explains intent, scope, and validation.
The author reviews the diff and confirms the CI status belongs to the latest commit.
Review feedback is concrete and tied to behavior or maintainability.
No secret is added to files or exposed to untrusted CI code.

items: Use focused branches to develop coherent changes before integration.
A useful PR explains why, what changed, how it was validated, and what remains risky.
Review behavior, edge cases, accessibility, testing, and maintainability rather than personal style preferences.
Merge and rebase produce different history shapes; coordinate before rewriting shared history.
CI provides repeatable evidence for a specific commit, not a guarantee that all behavior is correct.

blocks.text: Deep dive: branch strategy, conflict resolution, and CI as a merge gate

A branch strategy should make collaboration and release risk manageable, not create ceremony for its own sake. Short-lived feature branches work well when changes are small and continuously integrated; release/hotfix branches can help when a team has explicit release trains. A pull request is a reviewable proposal, while CI is repeatable evidence that selected checks passed on a specific commit—not proof that every product requirement is correct.

items: State the user problem and observable outcome in the PR description; link the issue or acceptance criteria.
Keep the diff focused. Remove accidental formatting churn and unrelated cleanup.
Review your own diff first; inspect deleted code, generated files, secrets and unexpected dependencies.
Require appropriate automated checks: install, lint, typecheck, unit/component tests and production build where the project supports them.
Ask reviewers to check correctness, edge cases, accessibility, error/loading/empty states and maintainability—not just formatting.
Resolve requested changes, rerun checks after the final code update, then merge according to branch protection and release policy.

steps.title: Recognize conflict markers
steps.explanation: HEAD and the incoming branch edited overlapping lines that Git could not safely combine automatically. The file is intentionally left in a conflicted state.

steps.title: Choose the intended behavior, not just one side
steps.explanation: Inspect the surrounding code and product requirement. The right result might be either title or a third deliberate value; blindly choosing ours or theirs may discard needed behavior.

steps.title: Verify the resolved file
steps.explanation: Remove all conflict markers, run the relevant tests and inspect the resulting diff. Mark the file resolved by staging it only after reviewing the final content.

blocks.text: Resolve a conflict and continue the operation safely

Conflict markers show that Git could not choose between overlapping edits; they do not tell you which product behavior is correct. First use `git status` to learn whether a merge or rebase is in progress. Read both sides and surrounding code, then produce the intended combined result and remove every marker. Review the diff, run `git diff --check` and relevant tests, and stage only the resolved paths. Continue the operation reported by Git: a merge and a rebase use different commands. If you cannot make a safe decision, stop and ask for context; abort only the operation that is actually in progress. Keep unrelated local work recoverable before starting a merge or rebase.

blocks.code:
git status
git diff -- src/components/PageTitle.tsx
# Resolve the conflict in the editor and remove every marker.
git diff --check
git add src/components/PageTitle.tsx
git status
git merge --continue

steps.title: Identify the operation and inspect the conflict
steps.explanation: Status tells you whether Git is merging or rebasing and which paths remain unmerged. Read the changed lines in context before editing.

steps.title: Create and check the intended result
steps.explanation: Edit the file so it satisfies the product requirement, remove all conflict markers, and use diff --check to catch whitespace errors. This command does not replace running tests.

steps.title: Stage and continue a merge
steps.explanation: Stage only the resolved path and verify status no longer lists it as unmerged. This example is for a merge in progress; use the rebase continuation command instead if status says a rebase is in progress.

blocks.code:
git status
git diff -- src/components/PageTitle.tsx
# Resolve the conflict in the editor and remove every marker.
git diff --check
git add src/components/PageTitle.tsx
git status
git rebase --continue

steps.title: Confirm that a rebase is in progress
steps.explanation: Do not infer the operation only from the file markers. Check status and inspect the commit being replayed and the conflicted file.

steps.title: Resolve the file and validate the diff
steps.explanation: Manually combine the intended changes, remove every marker and inspect the result. diff --check catches whitespace issues but not application logic defects.

steps.title: Stage and continue the rebase
steps.explanation: Stage the resolved path and check status. Use rebase --continue only while a rebase is active; do not also run merge --continue. Run tests after the operation completes.

items: When a merge is in progress, stage the resolved files and use `git merge --continue`.
When a rebase is in progress, stage the resolved files and use `git rebase --continue`; do not run both continuation commands.

If you cannot safely resolve a merge, `git merge --abort` attempts to return to the pre-merge state. For an active rebase, `git rebase --abort` returns to the original branch state for that rebase. Use only the command matching the operation reported by status.
Do not use a blanket `--ours` / `--theirs` checkout, `git reset --hard`, or deleting `.git` as a generic conflict fix; these can discard legitimate work or repository history.
After the operation completes, inspect `git status` and the final diff, run relevant tests, and push or open the pull request according to the team's branch policy.

blocks.prompt: You resolved the conflicted file, removed all markers, staged the result, and `git status` says a rebase is in progress. Which command continues that operation?

options.text: git rebase --continue
options.feedback: Correct. The status says a rebase is active. Continue that rebase only after reviewing and staging the resolved result.

options.text: git merge --continue
options.feedback: That command continues an in-progress merge, not a rebase. Choose the command matching the operation in status.

options.text: git push --force immediately
options.feedback: Publishing does not resolve the active local operation and a force push can rewrite shared history. Complete and validate the operation first.

options.text: git reset --hard HEAD
options.feedback: A hard reset can discard tracked changes and is not the generic next step after resolving a conflict.

blocks.explanation: The continuation command is determined by the operation Git reports. Resolve, inspect and stage the result first; use merge --continue for a merge and rebase --continue for a rebase.

blocks.title: Resolve and verify a merge or rebase conflict
blocks.context: This is a reasoning exercise, not an embedded terminal. In a practice repository, Git stopped because `PageTitle.tsx` contains overlapping edits. Your task is to preserve the intended combined behavior and finish the operation safely.
instructions: Read `git status` and identify whether Git is in a merge or rebase; inspect the conflicted file and relevant surrounding code.
Resolve the file according to the stated product requirement, remove every conflict marker and inspect the complete diff.
Run `git diff --check`, stage only the resolved path, and confirm it is no longer listed as unmerged.
Choose only the matching continuation command: `git merge --continue` for a merge or `git rebase --continue` for a rebase.
After the operation finishes, run relevant tests and inspect status and history. Explain when aborting is safer than guessing.
requirements: The resolution is based on intended behavior, not an automatic preference for ours or theirs.
No conflict markers remain and only intended paths are staged.
The continuation command matches the active merge/rebase operation.
The result is reviewed and relevant tests run after the operation completes.
No hard reset or force push is used as a generic shortcut; any abort is justified and matches the operation.

blocks.title: A green CI run is commit-specific
blocks.text: A check result applies to the commit and workflow that ran it. If you push another commit after a green run, confirm that required checks ran again on the new head. CI does not replace code review, product acceptance, security review, or a runtime test the pipeline does not perform.

blocks.prompt: You resolve a merge conflict locally and then make one more edit before pushing. What should you verify before merging the PR?

options.text: The previous green CI run is sufficient because the branch already passed once
options.feedback: That run tested an earlier commit. The final edit may introduce a new failure.

options.text: The conflict markers are gone, the diff is reviewed, and required checks passed for the current head
options.feedback: The final content and the exact commit awaiting merge must both be reviewed and checked.

options.text: Only the number of changed lines matters
options.feedback: Diff size can aid review, but it does not establish correctness or validate the latest commit.

options.text: Delete the failing test until merge succeeds
options.feedback: Removing a test to bypass a failure hides evidence rather than addressing the cause.

blocks.explanation: Review the final diff and verify status on the exact commit to be merged.

List the CI gates that this project should run before merge.
Explain why a green run from an earlier commit is not sufficient after the final edit.

The solution is justified from requirements rather than chosen by branch name alone.

blocks.text: Choose a branch strategy to fit the team's release rhythm

A branch model is a collaboration policy, not a Git feature that every project must adopt identically. Prefer the smallest process that lets a team integrate frequently, protect the default branch, test changes, and release safely. Long-lived branches accumulate divergence and make merges harder; short-lived branches still need tests and review.

items: Trunk-based development keeps branches very short-lived and integrates to a shared trunk frequently, often with feature flags and strong automated checks.
GitHub Flow normally uses a protected main branch, a short-lived feature branch, a pull request, checks, review, and merge.
Git Flow adds long-lived develop and purpose-specific release/hotfix branches. It can help with scheduled or parallel release maintenance, but it introduces more coordination and branch management.
A release branch stabilizes a candidate for a release; a hotfix branch isolates an urgent correction. Their source, target and back-merge policy should be explicit.
Choose based on release cadence, team size, support obligations and the maturity of CI. Do not adopt extra branches just because a diagram contains them.

blocks.text: Semantic Versioning communicates compatibility

For a public versioned API that follows Semantic Versioning, the release shape is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. At version 1.4.2, a backwards-compatible bug fix can become 1.4.3; a backwards-compatible feature can become 1.5.0; and an incompatible public API change generally requires 2.0.0. Pre-1.0.0 software may change its public API more freely under the SemVer specification, so document your project's policy.

blocks.caption: Illustrative changes from version 1.4.2
blocks.code:
1.4.2 -> 1.4.3  # backwards-compatible bug fix (PATCH)
1.4.2 -> 1.5.0  # backwards-compatible feature (MINOR)
1.4.2 -> 2.0.0  # incompatible public API change (MAJOR)

blocks.prompt: A library is at version 1.4.2 and releases a backwards-incompatible public API change. Under Semantic Versioning, which version is the expected next release?

options.feedback: PATCH is for backwards-compatible bug fixes, not a breaking public API change.
MINOR is for backwards-compatible new functionality, not a breaking public API change.
A backwards-incompatible public API change increments MAJOR.
Build metadata does not communicate a breaking compatibility change.

blocks.explanation: For a public stable API, SemVer uses MAJOR for incompatible changes, MINOR for backwards-compatible features, and PATCH for backwards-compatible fixes.

blocks.text: Continuous delivery and continuous deployment differ at release

Continuous integration (CI) repeatedly integrates changes and runs checks. In continuous delivery, the pipeline keeps a tested candidate deployable, but a person or release policy may still approve production. In continuous deployment, every change that passes the required gates is automatically released to production. Teams use these terms differently, so document the actual trigger. Branch protection is a repository-hosting rule that can require CI status and review before merge; CI reports evidence, while branch protection enforces the gate.

blocks.code:
Feature commit pushed
        ↓
CI: install → lint → typecheck → tests → build
        ↓
Checks green? ── no → inspect failure, fix, push new commit
        │ yes
        ↓
Branch protection: required review + required checks
        ↓
Merge to protected main
        ↓
Build immutable release artifact
        ↓
Continuous delivery: approval/release trigger → production
Continuous deployment: automatic gate → production

steps.title: Run checks against the proposed commit
steps.explanation: CI produces evidence for one tested SHA. A red check blocks progress until its cause is understood, corrected, and rerun on a new commit.

steps.title: Enforce policy at the merge boundary
steps.explanation: Branch protection can require human review and check statuses before accepting a merge. CI itself does not prevent a merge unless repository rules enforce the result.

steps.title: Name the production trigger accurately
steps.explanation: Continuous delivery keeps a release ready but can require approval. Continuous deployment automatically releases qualifying changes after gates. Keep the artifact and release process explicit so the same tested build is promoted.

blocks.text: Diagnose a failed stage from its logs

items: If `npm ci` fails, inspect the lockfile, Node/npm versions, `engines` constraints and registry error. Do not replace `npm ci` with `npm install` merely to hide a lockfile mismatch.
If lint or typecheck fails, locate the first relevant file and line, fix the cause, and run the corresponding command locally when the environment is available.
If a test fails, compare expected and actual behavior and decide whether it conflicts with the intended change or exposed a regression. Do not delete a test just to turn the status green.
If the production build fails, inspect compile errors, imports, environment variables, or the bundle budget. Passing tests does not prove that a release build can be produced.

If code checks are green but a Deploy Preview or production deployment is red, inspect its separate deploy job: build command, publish directory, environment, base path, redirects, and host-platform errors.
After fixing the cause, create a new commit and verify the new run against its exact SHA. An older green run does not validate code pushed later.

blocks.prompt: CI fails at `npm run build` even though install, lint, typecheck and tests passed. What should you do first?

options.text: Open the failed build-step log for the current SHA and fix the specific compilation, configuration or environment error.
options.feedback: Diagnose the stage that actually failed. After the fix, verify the new commit and its CI run.

options.text: Force-merge the PR because the tests passed.
options.feedback: The production build is a separate check. Its failure may mean the application cannot be built for release.

options.text: Upgrade all dependencies without inspecting the log.
options.feedback: A blind broad upgrade does not identify the root cause and may introduce additional incompatibilities.

options.text: Repeat an older green run and treat it as proof for the latest commit.
options.feedback: CI is tied to a specific SHA. Fix the cause first, then obtain a result for the new commit.

blocks.explanation: Read the failing step's logs, fix the observed cause, and verify the new SHA.

blocks.prompt: A pipeline runs all checks and creates a production-ready artifact, but an authorized person must approve the release. Which term most closely describes this release model?

options.text: Continuous delivery
options.feedback: The change remains deployable, but a human or release-policy trigger still starts production release.

options.text: Continuous deployment
options.feedback: Continuous deployment automatically releases every change that satisfies its gates.

options.text: Continuous integration only
options.feedback: The pipeline also prepares a release candidate; CI describes frequent integration and automated checks.

options.text: Branch protection
options.feedback: Branch protection governs merge conditions, not whether production release is manual or automatic.

blocks.explanation: Ask what triggers production: an approval/release action indicates delivery; automatic production release after gates indicates deployment.

items.title: Git Book: Branching and Basic Branching
